newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian tax vote plan draws criticism.
newsitem.headline: Australian tax vote plan draws criticism.

text.p: An Australian government proposal to hold a national vote on introducing a value-added tax was dismissed as silly and confused on Monday.
Australian Defence Force Academy political commentator Malcolm Mackerras also said he expected the government to abandon its push for a goods and services tax in the face of voter resistance.

The conservative Liberal-National government, gearing up for a dramatic overhaul of the country's outdated tax system, has flagged the possibility of a non-binding national vote on whether it should introduce a goods a services tax, a value-added tax on consumption.
The government has said a national vote on a GST was one option being considered in its plan to reform the tax system.
But the Labor opposition, political commentators and even some of the government's own members attacked the plan.
"This is a government sleepwalking in complete confusion on taxation matters, employment matters and just about everything else," opposition leader Kim Beazley told reporters.

Beazley would not say if legislation for a tax vote would pass parliament's upper house, the Senate, where the government needs the support of at least two non-government senators to pass legislation.
But Mackerras said he expected leftist non-government parties would block such a measure.
"It's a very silly idea, for a start the Senate would not pass the legislation to do this," he told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Government backbenchers were cautious about a possibile vote as they arrived for parliament on Monday, expressing concern about problems of cost and framing the question.
Senior Liberal Party parliamentarian Wilson Tuckey said he favoured a parliamentary inquiry into tax reform.
The government favours a goods and services tax -- which is applied at each stage of production, like European value-added taxes -- and reducing or abolishing a range of other indirect taxes.
But it remains committed to not imposing a goods and services tax in its first three-year term.

The coalition won power in 1996 after dropping an earlier policy to levy a 15 percent goods and services tax -- a policy widely blamed for the conservatives losing what was regarded as an unloseable election in 1993.
Mackerras said he expected the government to again campaign in the next election, due by mid-1999, on its winning 1996 pledge of no new taxes or tax increases.

"I do not expect that the government will go to the people promising a GST, simply because they couldn't win in the midst of a recession from opposition against an unpopular prime minister (in 1993)."
